title: Fortune cookies are Japanese-American
hook: The fortune cookie you get in a Chinese restaurant has roots in Japan.
peek: Most people link fortune cookies with Chinese food, but they are almost unknown in China. Their ancestor is a Japanese cracker from around Kyoto, and they were first sold in California by Japanese-American bakers.
lede: Fortune cookies come with the bill in Chinese restaurants across the United States, yet they are rarely seen in China. Their ancestor appears to be tsujiura senbei, a Japanese cracker with a paper fortune tucked into its fold, made by family bakeries around Kyoto. In the early 1900s, Japanese immigrant bakers in California started making a sweeter version.

bullets.text: The Japanese researcher Yasuko Nakamachi tracked down bakeries near Kyoto still making the older crackers, and found an 1878 book illustration of a man baking them. The Japanese version is larger, browner and flavoured with sesame and miso.

Hagiwara, who ran the Japanese Tea Garden in San Francisco's Golden Gate Park, is often credited with serving them in the early 1900s. Bakers in Los Angeles have made rival claims, and the true first is unknown.

During the Second World War, Japanese Americans were forced into internment camps, and Chinese American manufacturers took over the trade. After the war the cookie became a fixture of Chinese restaurants.
In 1983 San Francisco held a mock trial over the cookie's birthplace and ruled for its own city. The judge was not a historian, and the case was more civic fun than evidence.
In 2005, 110 people won a Powerball second prize in the same draw. Officials found many had played the lucky numbers printed on fortune cookie slips from the same New York factory.
